_description: CropCare AI — Disease Knowledge Base. All information sourced from agricultural university extension services and government agencies.

symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety lesions on leaves
Scabby, corky spots on fruit surface
Premature leaf drop in severe infections
Distorted or cracked fruit when infected early
Apple___Apple_scab.cause: Fungal spores overwinter in fallen leaves and are released during spring rains. Infection is favoured by cool, wet weather (15–24°C with prolonged leaf wetness).
organic_treatment: Apply sulphur-based fungicide sprays during early season
Use neem oil sprays (0.3%) during early infection stages
Apply Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a preventive foliar spray
chemical_treatment: Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L at green tip and pink bud stages
Myclobutanil (Systhane) at 0.5 mL/L at petal fall
Captan 50% WP at 2 g/L as a cover spray every 10–14 days
prevention: Remove and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce inoculum
Prune trees to improve air circulation
Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Goldrush)
Avoid overhead irrigation
Apple___Apple_scab.nutrient_notes: Balanced fertilisation; excess nitrogen promotes succulent growth susceptible to infection.

symptoms: Frogeye leaf spots: tan centres with purple margins
Firm, dark-brown to black rot expanding from the calyx end of fruit
Cankers on branches with reddish-brown sunken bark
Apple___Black_rot.cause: Fungal spores spread from mummified fruit and cankers during warm, wet weather (20–30°C). Infection occurs through wounds and natural openings.
organic_treatment: Prune out all cankered branches and remove mummified fruit
Apply copper-based fungicides (Bordeaux mixture 1%) before bud break
Neem oil sprays at 0.3% concentration during growing season
chemical_treatment: Captan 50% WP at 2 g/L during early season sprays
Thiophanate-methyl (Topsin-M) at 1 g/L for canker treatment
Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L as protective cover spray
prevention: Remove and destroy all mummified fruit and cankered wood
Maintain proper tree hygiene with regular pruning
Avoid wounding trees during cultivation
Harvest fruit promptly at maturity
Apple___Black_rot.nutrient_notes: Ensure adequate potassium to strengthen cell walls and improve disease resistance.

symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surface
Small tube-like projections (aecia) on leaf undersides
Spots may have a red border and develop black pycnia
Fruit lesions with raised, orange pustules
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cause: Requires two hosts (cedar/juniper and apple) to complete its life cycle. Spores from cedar galls are wind-dispersed to apple during wet spring weather.
organic_treatment: Remove nearby cedar and juniper trees within 100 m if feasible
Apply sulphur-based sprays from pink bud through petal fall
Bordeaux mixture (1%) applied at green tip stage
chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil (Systhane) at 0.5 mL/L from pink bud to 2 weeks after petal fall
Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L as protective spray
Propiconazole (Tilt) at 0.5 mL/L during high-risk periods
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Redfree)
Remove cedar galls from nearby juniper/cedar hosts in winter
Maintain good air circulation through pruning
Monitor for early symptoms and act promptly
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.nutrient_notes: Adequate potassium and phosphorus promote plant defence mechanisms.

symptoms: No disease symptoms. Leaves are uniformly green with no spots or lesions.
organic_treatment: No treatment needed. Continue with good agricultural practices.
chemical_treatment: No treatment needed.
prevention: Maintain regular pruning and sanitation
Follow an integrated pest management (IPM) schedule
Ensure balanced nutrition and adequate irrigation
Apple___healthy.nutrient_notes: Continue balanced NPK fertilisation appropriate for the growth stage.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.disease: Cercospora Leaf Spot / Gray Leaf Spot
symptoms: Small, rectangular, grey to tan lesions running parallel to leaf veins
Lesions may coalesce, causing large areas of leaf blight
Lower leaves usually affected first
Severe infection reduces photosynthetic area significantly
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.cause: Fungal spores survive on infected corn residue. Warm (25–30°C), humid conditions with extended dew periods favour infection. Continuous corn and reduced tillage increase risk.
organic_treatment: Crop rotation with non-host crops (legumes, cereals) for 1–2 years
Incorporate crop residue to accelerate decomposition
Apply Trichoderma-based biocontrol agents
chemical_treatment: Propiconazole (Tilt) at 0.5 mL/L applied at VT/R1 stage
Azoxystrobin (Amistar) at 0.5 mL/L at tasseling
Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L for early-season protection
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids (check local university ratings)
Practice crop rotation to break the disease cycle
Tillage to bury infected residue
Avoid excessive plant density
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.nutrient_notes: Adequate potassium reduces susceptibility. Avoid excess nitrogen which promotes dense canopy and humidity.

symptoms: Small, circular to elongated, cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules may be surrounded by a chlorotic halo
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and die prematurely
Pustules break through the epidermis releasing powdery rust-coloured spores
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.cause: Urediniospores are wind-dispersed from southern regions. Cool to moderate temperatures (16–23°C) with high humidity favour infection. Dew is necessary for spore germination.
organic_treatment: Plant resistant hybrids (most effective control method)
Remove volunteer corn plants that may harbour the pathogen
Apply neem oil (0.3%) during early infection
chemical_treatment: Propiconazole (Tilt) at 0.5 mL/L at first sign of pustules
Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L applied pre-tassel if epidemic expected
Azoxystrobin + propiconazole combination at recommended rates
prevention: Use rust-resistant hybrids
Early planting to avoid peak spore arrival
Monitor fields regularly during cool, humid weather
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilisation
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.nutrient_notes: Potassium deficiency increases susceptibility. Ensure balanced K nutrition.

symptoms: Long (2.5–15 cm), elliptical, greyish-green to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions may coalesce under severe conditions, blighting entire leaves
Lower leaves are typically affected first
Dark fungal sporulation visible on lesions during humid weather
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.cause: Spores survive on corn debris. Moderate temperatures (18–27°C) with heavy dew or rain promote infection. Continuous corn cropping and no-till increase inoculum.
organic_treatment: Crop rotation with non-host crops for at least 1 year
Deep ploughing to bury infected residue
Apply Trichoderma harzianum biocontrol agent
chemical_treatment: Propiconazole at 0.5 mL/L at disease onset
Azoxystrobin (Amistar) at 0.5 mL/L during tasseling
Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L as protective early-season spray
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids with Ht genes
Rotate crops and manage residue
Avoid late planting and excessive plant populations
Scout fields regularly from V8 onward
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.nutrient_notes: Balanced nitrogen and potassium. Excess N can increase canopy density and humidity, promoting disease.

symptoms: No disease symptoms. Leaves are uniformly green with no lesions.
organic_treatment: No treatment needed. Continue with good agricultural practices.
chemical_treatment: No treatment needed.
prevention: Practice crop rotation
Use certified disease-free seed
Maintain balanced soil fertility
Monitor fields regularly
Corn_(maize)___healthy.nutrient_notes: Continue recommended NPK programme for the growth stage.

symptoms: Dark brown to black concentric ring lesions ('target spots') on older leaves
Lesions often surrounded by a yellow halo
Lower leaves are affected first; progresses upward
Tubers may develop dark, sunken, circular lesions
Potato___Early_blight.cause: Fungus survives in soil and on plant debris. Warm temperatures (24–29°C), alternating wet and dry periods, and stressed or senescing plants favour infection.
organic_treatment: Apply Bordeaux mixture (1%) every 7–10 days during favourable conditions
Neem oil sprays at 0.3% at early symptom appearance
Trichoderma viride soil application before planting
chemical_treatment: Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L every 7–10 days
Chlorothalonil (Kavach) at 2 g/L as protective spray
Azoxystrobin (Amistar) at 0.5 mL/L for curative action
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers
Practice 2–3 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation
Ensure adequate spacing for air circulation
Potato___Early_blight.nutrient_notes: Adequate nitrogen and potassium reduce susceptibility. Avoid nitrogen deficiency which accelerates leaf senescence.

symptoms: Water-soaked, pale-green to dark-brown lesions on leaf margins and tips
White, cottony sporulation on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid browning and death of entire leaves and stems
Brown, firm rot on tubers extending inward
Potato___Late_blight.cause: Oomycete pathogen favoured by cool (10–20°C), wet conditions with prolonged leaf wetness. Spores are wind-dispersed and can cause epidemics rapidly. Historically responsible for the Irish Potato Famine (1845).
organic_treatment: Bordeaux mixture (1%) applied preventively every 5–7 days during wet weather
Copper hydroxide 77% WP at 2 g/L
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
chemical_treatment: Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold MZ) at 2.5 g/L every 7–10 days
Cymoxanil + Mancozeb (Curzate M) at 3 g/L
Dimethomorph (Acrobat) at 1 g/L for resistant strains
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars (e.g., Kufri Jyoti, Kufri Girdhari in India)
Use certified disease-free seed tubers
Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles
Avoid irrigation during cool, cloudy periods
Hill up tubers to prevent tuber infection from surface spores
Potato___Late_blight.nutrient_notes: Avoid excess nitrogen which promotes lush, susceptible growth. Adequate potassium improves resistance. Phosphorus supports root health.

symptoms: No disease symptoms. Leaves are uniformly green and turgid.
organic_treatment: No treatment needed.
chemical_treatment: No treatment needed.
prevention: Use certified seed tubers
Practice crop rotation
Maintain proper soil moisture and fertility
Scout fields regularly
Potato___healthy.nutrient_notes: Follow recommended potato fertilisation schedule (typically 120-80-80 N-P-K kg/ha).

symptoms: Small, water-soaked, dark spots on leaves, stems and fruit
Leaf spots may be angular with yellow halos
Spots on fruit are raised, scab-like with cracked centres
Severe infections cause defoliation
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacterium spreads via contaminated seed, splashing rain and overhead irrigation. Warm (24–30°C), humid conditions favour rapid spread.
organic_treatment: Copper-based bactericides (copper hydroxide 77% WP at 2 g/L) every 7–10 days
Bordeaux mixture (1%) applied preventively
Remove and destroy severely infected plants
chemical_treatment: Copper hydroxide + mancozeb tank mix (2 + 2.5 g/L)
Streptocycline (streptomycin sulfate) at 100 ppm (where registered)
Kasugamycin at 0.2 mL/L as an alternative antibiotic
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Hot-water treat seed (50°C for 25 minutes)
Practice crop rotation (2–3 years) with non-solanaceous crops
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip systems
Disinfect tools and stakes between uses
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.nutrient_notes: Avoid excess nitrogen which produces succulent tissues susceptible to infection. Calcium helps strengthen cell walls.

symptoms: Concentric ring ('target spot') lesions on lower leaves first
Lesions surrounded by yellow halos
Stem lesions appear as dark, sunken cankers at the soil line
Fruit may develop dark, leathery spots near the stem end
Tomato___Early_blight.cause: Fungal spores survive in soil and plant debris. Warm temperatures (24–29°C) with alternating wet and dry conditions, and nutrient-stressed or ageing plants favour infection.
organic_treatment: Bordeaux mixture (1%) every 7–10 days
Neem oil at 0.3% during early infection
Trichoderma viride applied to soil and as foliar spray
chemical_treatment: Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L every 7–10 days
Chlorothalonil at 2 g/L as cover spray
Azoxystrobin at 0.5 mL/L for curative action
prevention: Mulch around plants to reduce soil splash
Remove lower leaves that contact the soil
Practice 2-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Stake or cage plants for better air circulation
Tomato___Early_blight.nutrient_notes: Adequate potassium and nitrogen reduce susceptibility. Avoid nitrogen deficiency.

symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked patches on leaves, often starting at leaf tips
White fungal growth visible on underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid browning and collapse of leaves and stems
Firm, greasy, brown rot on fruit
Tomato___Late_blight.cause: Cool (10–20°C), wet conditions with prolonged leaf wetness. Spores are wind-dispersed over long distances. Spreads extremely rapidly under favourable conditions.
organic_treatment: Bordeaux mixture (1%) every 5–7 days during wet weather
Copper hydroxide 77% WP at 2 g/L
Immediately remove and destroy infected plants
chemical_treatment: Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold MZ) at 2.5 g/L
Cymoxanil + Mancozeb at 3 g/L
Chlorothalonil at 2 g/L as protective spray
prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation
Ensure good air circulation (wider spacing, pruning)
Remove volunteer tomato and potato plants
Scout fields daily during cool, wet weather
Tomato___Late_blight.nutrient_notes: Reduce nitrogen application. Adequate phosphorus and potassium improve resistance. Avoid waterlogging.

symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow spots on upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown velvety mold on lower leaf surface
Affected leaves may curl, wither, and drop
Most common in greenhouse and high-tunnel production
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cause: High humidity (>85%) and moderate temperatures (22–24°C) favour infection. Poor air circulation in enclosed growing structures is a major risk factor.
organic_treatment: Improve ventilation and reduce humidity in greenhouses
Bordeaux mixture (1%) at first sign of symptoms
Neem oil sprays at 0.3%
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil at 2 g/L every 7–10 days
Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L
Azoxystrobin at 0.5 mL/L
prevention: Ensure adequate ventilation in greenhouses/tunnels
Space plants widely to promote air circulation
Avoid wetting foliage during irrigation
Use resistant cultivars carrying Cf resistance genes
Remove infected leaves promptly
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.nutrient_notes: Balanced nutrition; excess nitrogen increases foliage density and humidity retention.

symptoms: Numerous small (2–3 mm), circular spots with dark margins and grey centres
Tiny black pycnidia (spore-producing bodies) visible in spot centres
Lower leaves affected first; severe infections cause extensive defoliation
Fruit is rarely directly affected but is susceptible to sunscald after defoliation
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungal spores survive on infected debris and solanaceous weeds. Warm (20–25°C) wet weather with splashing rain promotes spread.
organic_treatment: Bordeaux mixture (1%) every 7 days during wet weather
Copper-based fungicides at first symptom appearance
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil at 2 g/L every 7–10 days
Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L
Azoxystrobin at 0.5 mL/L for systemic control
prevention: Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash
Practice crop rotation (2–3 years)
Remove solanaceous weeds
Stake plants and prune lower branches
Avoid overhead irrigation
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.nutrient_notes: Adequate potassium and calcium strengthen plant defences.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.pathogen: Tetranychus urticae (arachnid pest, not a pathogen)
symptoms: Tiny yellow or white stippling on upper leaf surface
Fine silk webbing on leaf undersides and between leaves
Leaves become bronzed, dry and brittle
Severe infestations cause leaf drop and reduced yield
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Hot (>27°C), dry conditions favour mite population explosions. Dusty conditions and use of broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators worsen infestations.
organic_treatment: Spray with water jets to dislodge mites
Apply neem oil at 0.3% every 5–7 days
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) as biological control
Apply insecticidal soap at 2% concentration
chemical_treatment: Abamectin (Vertimec) at 0.5 mL/L, targeting leaf undersides
Spiromesifen (Oberon) at 0.3 mL/L
Dicofol 18.5 EC at 2.5 mL/L (where registered)
prevention: Monitor plants regularly, especially during hot, dry weather
Maintain adequate irrigation to reduce plant stress
Avoid dusty field conditions by mulching or cover-cropping
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill mite predators
Interplant with companion crops that attract beneficial insects
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.nutrient_notes: Stressed, nitrogen-deficient plants are more susceptible. Maintain balanced nutrition.

symptoms: Small, dark-brown circular spots with concentric rings (target pattern)
Spots enlarge and may develop a pale tan centre
Primarily affects lower and middle leaves
Severe infections cause extensive defoliation and fruit lesions
Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Warm (20–32°C), humid conditions favour infection. The fungus persists in soil and plant debris. Dense canopy and poor air circulation increase risk.
organic_treatment: Bordeaux mixture (1%) at first symptom appearance
Remove and destroy infected leaves
Trichoderma-based biocontrol agents applied to soil
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil at 2 g/L every 7 days
Azoxystrobin at 0.5 mL/L
Difenoconazole at 0.5 mL/L
prevention: Prune lower branches and maintain adequate plant spacing
Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Mulch to reduce soil splash
Avoid overhead irrigation
Remove plant debris after harvest
Tomato___Target_Spot.nutrient_notes: Balanced fertilisation; excess nitrogen promotes dense canopy conducive to disease.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (Begomovirus, family Geminiviridae)
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaves
Yellowing of leaf margins, especially on new growth
Stunted plant growth with shortened internodes
Flower drop and drastically reduced fruit set
Plants infected early may be completely unproductive
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: Transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci (silverleaf whitefly). The virus is acquired and transmitted in a persistent, circulative manner. Hot seasons and high whitefly populations drive epidemics.
organic_treatment: Install yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce whitefly populations
Apply neem oil (0.3%) or neem seed kernel extract (5%) to repel whiteflies
Release Encarsia formosa parasitoid wasps for biological whitefly control
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
chemical_treatment: Imidacloprid (Confidor) at 0.3 mL/L as soil drench or foliar spray for whitefly control
Thiamethoxam (Actara) at 0.25 g/L for whitefly control
No direct chemical cure for the virus; control is via vector management
prevention: Use TYLCV-resistant tomato varieties (e.g., carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, Ty-3 genes)
Use fine-mesh insect-proof netting in nurseries and greenhouses
Implement a whitefly-free period before transplanting
Remove weed hosts that harbour the virus or whiteflies
Avoid planting new tomato crops adjacent to older infected ones
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.nutrient_notes: Virus-infected plants have reduced nutrient uptake. Foliar micronutrient sprays (Zn, Fe, Mn) may help maintain vigour in mildly affected plants.

symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic mottling pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion, curling and fern-like appearance (shoestring leaves)
Stunted plant growth
Uneven ripening and brown (internal browning) on fruit
Reduced fruit yield
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Highly stable virus transmitted mechanically through contaminated hands, tools, clothing, and seed. Does NOT require an insect vector. Survives in plant debris and on surfaces for months to years.
organic_treatment: No cure once infected. Remove and destroy infected plants.
Dip hands and tools in skimmed milk (10%) before handling plants (protein in milk inactivates the virus)
Cross-protection with mild strains (experimental, not widely recommended)
chemical_treatment: No chemical treatment available for viral infections
Prevention and sanitation are the only effective approaches
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and transplants
Use resistant varieties carrying the Tm-2² resistance gene
Wash hands thoroughly with soap before handling plants
Disinfect tools with 10% bleach or trisodium phosphate solution
Do not smoke near tomato plants (tobacco mosaic virus cross-infection)
Remove and destroy infected plants and debris
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.nutrient_notes: Maintain balanced nutrition to support plant vigour. No specific nutrient adjustments for viral control.

symptoms: No disease symptoms. Leaves are uniformly green and vigorous.
organic_treatment: No treatment needed.
chemical_treatment: No treatment needed.
prevention: Continue integrated pest management (IPM) practices
Maintain balanced fertilisation
Scout fields regularly for early detection
Practice crop rotation
Tomato___healthy.nutrient_notes: Follow recommended tomato fertilisation (typically 120-60-60 N-P₂O₅-K₂O kg/ha).
